opus-5.5.text:
It's a great question, and I think there's a common misconception that instruction fine-tuning is "cheap" in an absolute sense. It's cheap relative to pretraining, for sure. Pretraining is where the overwhelming majority of the compute goes: you're processing trillions of tokens, you're running for weeks or months on thousands of accelerators. Instruction fine-tuning, by comparison, might touch a dataset that's orders of magnitude smaller, so in terms of raw FLOPs it's a tiny fraction of the overall budget.

But I think that framing hides a few important things. The first is that the cost of fine-tuning scales with the size of the model you're starting from. If you're doing full fine-tuning on a model with tens or hundreds of billions of parameters, you still need to hold those weights, the gradients, and the optimizer states in memory. So the memory footprint, and the infrastructure you need to coordinate that, is not trivial, even if the number of steps is small. That's a big reason why so much work has gone into parameter-efficient methods: adapters, LoRA-style approaches, only updating a subset of weights. Those dramatically reduce the memory and compute overhead and make fine-tuning accessible to a much wider set of researchers.

The second thing is that fine-tuning isn't a one-shot event the way people sometimes imagine. In practice you're iterating: you're trying different data mixtures, different templates, different languages, you're running ablations, you're evaluating. So the aggregate compute across all those experiments can add up quite a bit. And if you're layering preference training or reinforcement learning from human feedback on top, the cost profile changes again, because now you may be running multiple models at once, generating samples, scoring them.

And then the third point, which is something I care a lot about, is that a lot of the real cost of instruction tuning isn't compute at all, it's data. Collecting high-quality, diverse instruction data, especially across many languages, is incredibly expensive in human time and coordination. That was very much our experience with the Aya project, where we worked with thousands of contributors across many languages. The compute to fine-tune was manageable; the effort to build data that actually represents the world was the hard part.

So my short answer is: pretraining dominates compute, but instruction tuning is where a lot of the leverage is. You get a disproportionate amount of behavior change for a relatively small amount of compute, which is exactly why it's such an interesting place to invest research effort, and why I think we should be thinking more carefully about data quality and efficiency there rather than just assuming bigger pretraining runs will solve everything.

r001.rationale: It contrasts pretraining on trillions of tokens over weeks or months with instruction fine-tuning on a dataset orders of magnitude smaller.

r002.rationale: It describes fine-tuning as much cheaper than pretraining and says practitioners can iterate across data mixtures, templates, languages, and ablations.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the comparison is actually one of the more interesting things to reflect on, because the numbers are almost absurd when you put them side by side. Pretraining is this enormous, one-time, capital-intensive event. You're talking about trillions of tokens, thousands of accelerators running for weeks or months, and a very small number of organizations in the world that can actually afford to do it. It's the thing that dominates the headlines when we talk about compute.

Instruction fine-tuning, by contrast, is tiny. It's often a fraction of a percent of the pretraining budget. You're typically working with tens of thousands to maybe a few million examples rather than trillions of tokens, and you're running for a relatively small number of steps. And with parameter-efficient methods like LoRA, you're not even updating most of the weights, so the memory footprint drops substantially too. So from a pure FLOPs standpoint, it's not really a comparison. Pretraining is the mountain and fine-tuning is a small hill at the base of it.

But I think the more interesting point is that the small compute footprint is a bit deceptive about where the difficulty lies. Pretraining is expensive but, in a sense, conceptually simple: next-token prediction over a huge corpus. Instruction fine-tuning is cheap in compute but expensive in human judgment. The quality of what you get is incredibly sensitive to the data. Who wrote the instructions, how diverse the tasks are, which languages are covered, how the examples were curated. We've seen in our own work that a few thousand very carefully constructed examples can move a model more than orders of magnitude more noisy data. So the scarce resource shifts from GPUs to people, to annotation, to taste about what good behavior looks like.

And there's one more thing I'd add, which is that the compute asymmetry has real consequences for who gets to shape these systems. Because fine-tuning is so cheap, it democratizes customization. Many groups can take a pretrained model and adapt it. But they're all adapting something whose fundamental capabilities and biases were set during a pretraining run they had no say in. So the gap in compute between the two stages is also a gap in power and influence over the technology, and I think that's worth being honest about when we talk about the economics of this.

r001.rationale: It contrasts pretraining on trillions of tokens over weeks or months with fine-tuning on far fewer examples and relatively few steps, communicating that pretraining takes longer because it processes much more data.

r002.rationale: It says fine-tuning’s low compute cost lets many groups customize models, but does not say that this enables more experimentation with different training configurations.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s useful to distinguish the total amount of compute from the hardware you need to participate. Pretraining is typically much more computationally expensive: you’re training over an enormous amount of data, often for a long time. Instruction fine-tuning starts with that pretrained model and uses a much smaller dataset, so the additional compute is usually a small fraction of pretraining.

But cheaper doesn’t necessarily mean accessible. You still have to fit the model into memory, and if you’re updating all its parameters, you also need memory for gradients and optimizer states. So even a relatively short fine-tuning run can require substantial hardware. Parameter-efficient methods can reduce that burden, but the distinction matters: the total compute cost can be much lower while the barrier to entry remains high.

r001.rationale: The response says pretraining uses an enormous amount of data and often runs for a long time, while instruction fine-tuning uses a much smaller dataset and less compute.

r002.rationale: It describes fine-tuning as requiring less compute, but does not connect that lower burden to being able to experiment with different training configurations.

sol-6.1.text:
Instruction fine-tuning is typically much less computationally demanding than pretraining. In pretraining, you’re learning from an enormous amount of data, and that’s where most of the compute goes. With instruction fine-tuning, you’re starting from those learned capabilities and using a much smaller dataset to shape how the model responds to instructions.

That doesn’t make it trivial—you still have to work with a very large model—but the computational budgets are quite different. And that’s an important distinction: a relatively small amount of additional training can have a substantial effect on how useful the model feels to someone interacting with it.

r001.rationale: It says pretraining uses an enormous amount of data while instruction fine-tuning uses a much smaller dataset, and describes their computational budgets as quite different, conveying why pretraining takes longer.

r002.rationale: It states that instruction fine-tuning is less computationally demanding, but does not say this enables more experimentation with different training configurations.
